chapter_theme: The second half of the patikam runs the story from Civakan's rescue by a god through his wanderings and marriages in the Pallava land, the Takka land and the middle country, his return to his mother, the killing of his enemy and his just rule, to his renunciation at the height of power, the renunciation of his whole household, and the closing verse in which a higher bliss makes women's pleasure unwanted.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by a merchant, who wins eight brides, regains his father's kingdom and renounces
the god who carries Civakan off from prison, frees him and teaches him spells
the merchant's daughter of the Takka land whom Civakan marries and leaves
the king of the middle country who receives Civakan
the lion-like royals of the middle country who keep Civakan and give him a princess in marriage
the merchant's daughter who vowed to look on no man and yields to Civakan
Civakan's wives, who renounce with him

16.reading: The god who carried Civakan off unties the flower-cord with which tireless soldiers had bound his arms, adorns him with fine jewels, bids him, as one of unfailing love, to think of him, teaches him fitting spells and sends him on his way.
16.nuance: The verse does not name the god; verse 15 calls him only a god (தேவன்) who came down like lightning. That he is the dog given nectar in verse 14 is the story's later telling, not the patikam's. The words நினைக்க (think, remember) set up the god as a helper to be called on in need, and the spells (விஞ்சை) are given, not earned.
16.event: The god frees Civakan from his bonds, adorns him, teaches him spells and sends him off.

17.reading: Civakan crosses the fragrant kanthal slopes where elephants sleep as Vishnu sleeps on his serpent bed, reaches the jewelled Pallava land hedged by dark hills, and enters its city of flags and naga groves.
17.nuance: Every line turns on நாகம் in a different sense (serpent, elephant, hill, the naga tree), a display of the poet's craft inside a bare plot summary. The image of Vishnu (மணி வண்ணன்) on the serpent bed is ornament in a Jain work and carries no claim.
17.event: Civakan travels over the hills and enters the city of the Pallava land.

18.reading: A snake, rising at the face of the city king's daughter as if it were the cool moon, bites her; Civakan, saying 'let not your heart melt', cures her and is joined with her.
18.nuance: The snake's mistake is a praise of her face, so the bite itself is a compliment. The cure is given only as a word of comfort (சித்தம் குழையற்க); the means is not named, though verse 16 has just given Civakan spells.
18.event: Civakan cures the Pallava king's daughter of a snakebite and marries her.

19.reading: Civakan delights in her for two months, then, with arms like jewelled pillars, cuts through the mountains and swiftly takes the road again.
19.nuance: The patikam gives union and departure in one verse, a pattern it repeats with the next bride: the hero never stays where he has won.
19.event: After two months with his new wife, Civakan leaves and crosses the mountains.

20.reading: Reaching the rich Takka land, Civakan is wasted within by the spear-eyed gaze of a merchant's daughter, lives with her as one life, and then leaves her of the fragrant garland.
20.nuance: The woman's eyes act on him (வாட்ட, waste), the language of love's wound, yet the line that joins them as one life is followed at once by his leaving.
20.event: In the Takka land Civakan marries a merchant's daughter and then leaves her.

21.reading: While her nectar-like eyes rain tears, Civakan crosses a forest of heavy rain, and the king of the middle country, seeing his terrible bow, comes out to receive him.
21.nuance: Line 3's வெள் வேலவன் (the one of the bright spear) may be Civakan or the king, and so who sees whose bow in line 4 is not fixed; the rain of her tears and the rain-forest he walks into are set side by side.
21.event: Civakan leaves his weeping wife, crosses a rain-forest and is received by the king of the middle country.

22.reading: The strong lion-like royals of the chariot kings, delighted at his bow and sword, keep him there under guard and give the girl whose eyes are a palmful wide to the young man of the burning spear.
22.nuance: Line 1 may mean the king's lion-like sons or the kings themselves, and கடி பெய்து may mean setting a guard or making the wedding; the reading turns on both.
22.event: The royals of the middle country, pleased with Civakan's skill in arms, keep him and give him a princess in marriage.

23.reading: His younger brother, desolate like the star that has lost the moon, comes to join him at the bidding of a woman; his friends gather to him; and Civakan leaves the city to bow before his mother.
23.nuance: Who the one 'fit to rise' (உதிதற்கு உரியாள்) is, and how the friends come 'by the way of treasure' (நிதியின் நெறியின்), the patikam does not explain; the story may mean Gandharvadattai's arts, but the verse does not name her. The brother's grief is likened to a star losing its moon, a bond in which the younger one shines only beside the elder.
23.event: Civakan's brother and friends rejoin him, and he leaves the city to bow before his mother.

24.reading: Having taken counsel with his mother, Civakan of the fragrant garland enters the sky-high streets of the city and falls into the great sea of nectar of a maiden born by a boon, a lamp upon the earth.
24.nuance: The counsel with the mother is the turn from wandering to the recovery of the kingdom. The maiden of lines 3 and 4 is not named; the order of the ilampakams makes her Vimalai, but the verse alone does not say so.
24.event: After consulting his mother, Civakan enters the city and falls in love with a maiden born by a boon.

25.reading: The girl named Suramanjari, a vine of endless pleasure, lowers her banner; and Civakan shoots the boar and kills the enemy so that all fear of him ends.
25.nuance: Line 4's நஞ்சு ஊறும் வேலான் (he of the poison-dripping spear) can be Civakan or the enemy he kills; the verse names neither the enemy nor the boar contest's prize. Suramanjari's lowered banner reverses the vow told in verse 13.
25.event: Suramanjari yields to Civakan; he shoots the boar target and kills his enemy.

26.reading: Civakan wins the nectar-like beauty of his maternal uncle's daughter, whose red, long eyes are like a spear drawn from a wound, and the cool shade of his moon-touching umbrella and just sceptre spreads over the land.
26.nuance: The cross-cousin marriage and the return of the just sceptre are given in one verse: the recovered kingdom and the last bride arrive together.
26.event: Civakan marries his uncle's daughter and rules with a just sceptre.

27.reading: While kings bring tribute, fortune stays, his just sceptre runs and his victories stand with every enemy chariot bowed, Civakan hears the dharma and, afraid of kingship like a snake struck by thunder, renounces at the feet of the Knower.
27.nuance: The renunciation comes at the height of rule, not after loss: lines 1 and 2 list everything a king could want. The motive given is fear of kingship itself (அரசு அஞ்சி), roused by hearing the dharma, and the snake struck by thunder makes the turn sudden and total. The teacher is named only அறிவன் (the Knower), a title for the omniscient one; the verse names no school and narrates the act rather than stating a rule, so no claim is recorded.
27.event: At the height of his reign Civakan hears the dharma and renounces kingship at the feet of the omniscient teacher.

28.reading: His younger brother with an army of elephants, chariots and sea-like horse, his friends and his richly adorned wives all renounce the things of sense, and Civakan, lord of the vina, goes to the state that is ever new.
28.nuance: The whole household goes with him: brother, friends and wives renounce together, so renunciation here is not a lone flight from kin. The goal is named only விருந்து ஆர் கதி (the state full of newness); whether it is a heaven or final release the verse does not fix, though the last ilampakam is named for release. Calling him வீணைக் கிழவன் at this moment recalls the vina contest by which he first won a bride.
28.event: Civakan's brother, friends and wives renounce, and Civakan attains the higher state.

29.reading: Like one who has eaten nectar from a mouth of honey, the prosperous one no longer wants the pleasure of women whose beauty makes the heavens bow; the poet says he will tell those here the flood of bliss Civakan attained, praised by all, as the patikam has set it out.
29.nuance: The simile reverses the usual order: Civakan does not give up women to win bliss; having tasted a greater sweetness, he no longer wants the lesser. This is told of Civakan, not laid down as a rule, so no claim is recorded. The closing words (பதிகத்துள் இயன்ற வாறே) end the summary that began at verse 9.
29.event: Civakan, no longer wanting the pleasures of women, attains a flood of bliss.

links.note: Verse 14 has Civakan give nectar to a dog dying in the bathing pool; verse 16 has a god free him, arm him with spells and ask to be remembered.
links.teaches: Set beside each other, the dying dog's gift and the god's rescue show the patikam placing a kindness and its return two verses apart, leaving the reader to see the debt repaid before the story names the god.

links.note: The spells the god gives in verse 16 are followed by the cure of a snakebite in verse 18, given only as a word of comfort.
links.teaches: The patikam never says how Civakan cures the princess, but read after verse 16 the cure is the god's gift at work, so his first marriage is won by the rescue, not by his own arms.

links.note: Verse 10 has the sword-eyed mother keep a vow that her son may live; in verse 23 the grown son, with brother and friends, comes to bow before her.
links.teaches: The mother's austerity, kept apart from her son, is answered when he returns alive to bow to her, and the patikam places that homecoming just before he turns to win back the kingdom she lost.

links.note: Verse 13 has Suramanjari, shamed over the scented powder, refuse to look on any male form and shut herself away; verse 25 has her lower her banner.
links.teaches: Read together, the two verses frame Suramanjari's vow against men as a challenge the plot exists to undo, so her yielding is told as a conquest like the boar and the enemy in the same verse.

links.note: Verse 9 tells how the king, sunk in desire and deaf to counsel, fell to a plot while the queen fled to the burning ground; verse 25 has the son kill the enemy.
links.teaches: The usurpation that verse 9 blames on the father's own desire and deafness to counsel is settled only by the son's killing, so the father's fault and the son's revenge frame the whole plot.

links.note: Verse 9 has Saccandan, steeped in desire, not hear counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்) and lose his throne; verse 27 has his son hear the dharma (அறம் கேட்டு) and give his throne up.
links.teaches: The patikam opens on a king ruined because he would not listen and closes on his son freed because he did, so hearing becomes the hinge between losing a kingdom and leaving one.

links.note: Civakan renounces kingship at its height after hearing the dharma; in the Manimekalai the minister tells the king who wants to leave his throne that the Buddha's dharma, which protects others' lives, is not that.
links.teaches: The two epics weigh the same act differently: the Cintamani's patikam praises a just king's leaving the throne once he hears the dharma, while the Manimekalai has a minister argue that a king who abandons the people he guards departs from the Buddha's dharma.

links.note: The Naladiyar's best of men renounce house, youth, wealth and strength because they see these do not last; Civakan renounces in full possession of all of them.
links.teaches: The quatrain grounds renunciation in seeing that goods pass away, while the epic's king renounces while every good still stands and gives fear of kingship, roused by the dharma, as his motive, so impermanence is not the only road to leaving.

gains.a: Civakan's sudden turn is set against the standard ethics-book reason, showing that his motive is moral fear of rule rather than loss
gains.b: the quatrain's list of passing goods is tested on a case where none of them has yet failed

links.note: The Kural asks what one who keeps household life in dharma could gain by going the outer way; in the Cintamani the whole household, brother, friends and wives, goes that way and reaches a higher state.
links.teaches: The Kural's question assumes a householder could gain nothing more by leaving, but the epic answers it by having a just king's whole household leave together and arrive at the state that is ever new.

gains.a: the epic's mass renunciation is read as an answer to a Tamil defence of household life, not only as story
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is shown to be contestable from inside Tamil literature, by a narrative that claims a gain beyond the householder's

links.note: The Kural's lover asks whether the lotus-eyed one's world can be sweeter than sleep in the beloved's soft arms; Civakan, having tasted a nectar-like bliss, no longer wants the pleasure of women whose beauty makes the heavens bow.
links.teaches: The lover ranks the beloved's arms above heaven, while the epic's hero, having tasted a higher bliss, finds women's embrace unwanted, so the two verses make opposite rankings of the same two goods.

gains.a: the patikam's closing simile gains an opponent: it reads as a rebuttal of the lover's ranking rather than a bare statement
gains.b: the couplet's open question gets an answer from a renouncer, showing what the lover's ranking denies

links.note: Verse 1 praises the god of gods who reached by himself (தன்னின் எய்தி) the supreme bliss that does not fail; verse 29 ends the patikam with Civakan in a flood of bliss (இன்ப வெள்ளம்).
links.teaches: The patikam opens on a god who won unfailing bliss by his own effort and closes on a man who reaches a flood of bliss, so the hero's whole story is framed as walking the road the worshipped one walked, not as receiving a gift from him.

links.note: Pattinathar asks what breasts, union with women and gathered wealth can do against the coming struggle, and says the god put an eyeless needle in his hand; Civakan stops wanting women's pleasure because he has tasted a greater sweetness.
links.teaches: Both rich men turn from women and wealth, but the Siddhar's ground is their uselessness before death and a sign from Siva, while the epic's is a higher bliss already tasted, so the same turn can be told as a loss seen through or as a lesser pleasure outgrown.

gains.a: the epic's sweet simile is set against a bitter Saiva account of the same turn, showing that the Cintamani makes renunciation a gain of pleasure, not a flight from it
gains.b: the Siddhar's turn, which rests on death and a god's token, is shown to be one motive among others, since a Jain hero leaves the same goods with no god sending a sign

source_issues: Verse 29 ends the patikam with a comma after இயன்ற வாறே where a full stop is expected.
